overview: Picture southwest China in 1650: a fugitive emperor moves between courts, former rebel generals command armies in his name, Qing forces press south, and families carry grain and news along mountain roads. The atlas calls this huge shape “Post-Ming Warlords,” but no single country with that name ruled it from 1650 to 1715. First came the Yongli Southern Ming court, shielded and constrained by commanders Sun Kewang and Li Dingguo. Counterattacks briefly recovered cities before rivalry and Qing invasion drove Yongli into Burma; Wu Sangui seized and executed him in 1662. Next, Wu and other former Ming officers governed southern feudatories for the Qing, then rebelled from 1673 to 1681. The atlas freezes one southwest polygon through both struggles and keeps it until 1715. Within that rough shape lived Han migrants and diverse Yi, Miao, Yao, Zhuang, Dai and other peoples under different local rulers. This card follows armies and courts, but also schools, farms, medicine, waterworks, families, art, toilets and one tiny coin whose four characters carried a very large claim.

periods.title: A court survives through military patrons
periods.summary: The Yongli emperor claimed Ming legitimacy, but former rebel commanders held much of the real military power in Yunnan and Guizhou. Flight, bargaining and fragile alliances shaped the first years inside the atlas interval.

periods.title: Anlong confinement and a loyalist counterattack
periods.summary: Sun Kewang moved Yongli to Anlong and controlled access to the court. Li Dingguo meanwhile defeated major Qing forces and recovered Guilin, giving a battered restoration movement a startling but temporary revival.

periods.title: Rival commanders split the restoration
periods.summary: Li Dingguo brought the emperor to Kunming, and conflict with Sun Kewang became open warfare. Sun defected to the Qing; coordinated invasion then broke the remaining inland defense and forced Yongli toward Burma.

periods.title: Exile and the political end of the Southern Ming court
periods.summary: Yongli took refuge in the Toungoo kingdom of Burma. Qing forces led by Wu Sangui compelled his surrender, carried him to Kunming and executed him in 1662, while other loyalist networks continued elsewhere.

periods.title: Qing feudatories dominate the south
periods.summary: Wu Sangui in Yunnan and powerful commanders in Guangdong and Fujian enjoyed armies, revenues and unusual autonomy as Qing clients. These were not a continuation of the Yongli state even though the atlas uses one label.

periods.title: Wu Sangui rebels and declares Zhou
periods.summary: An imperial plan to reduce the feudatories triggered revolt. Wu gained allies and advanced into the Yangzi region, then proclaimed a Zhou dynasty in 1678. Other feudatories shifted sides as the war changed.

periods.title: Death, retreat and defeat
periods.summary: Wu Sangui died in 1678. Rebel power contracted toward Yunnan, where Qing and loyal Green Standard forces completed the campaign in late 1681. The inland regime represented by the later half of this card was over.

periods.title: The atlas shape outlives its historical subjects
periods.summary: The unchanged polygon remains on the 1700 map and disappears only at 1715. Historically Qing consolidation, reconstruction and local negotiation filled these decades; no post-Ming warlord state survived to the drawn endpoint.

sections.title: Audit the atlas before believing the border

items.text: The exact live record is id “post-ming-warlords,” label “Post-Ming Warlords,” circa 1650 to 1715. Its coverage ledger classifies it as a state with two border intervals and, before this packet, no summary, card or review. The label is an atlas category, not a name used by one historical government.

At 1650 the target is a MultiPolygon with two parts, two rings and 166 positions. Its bounds are 97.523° to 116.085° east and 18.097° to 28.839° north. The coordinate SHA-256 is b32847b1355f4dc47a2d9ed2b13eb16ecce5ee3ce139ae2cf76086498e2085d1. Those decimals fingerprint display data; they do not make the politics precise.

The large part covers broad swaths of Yunnan, Guizhou, Guangxi and western Guangdong; the small part traces Hainan. Point tests place Guangzhou, Zhaoqing, Guilin, Nanning, Guiyang, Kunming and Tengchong inside, while Beijing, Nanjing, Fuzhou, Xiamen, Chengdu, Chongqing, Lijiang, Tainan and Hanoi fall outside.

The 1700 target has exactly the same type, positions, bounds and coordinate hash as 1650. A frozen fifty-year shape cannot show the Yongli court’s retreat, the feudatories’ shifting front or the Qing recovery. It is a broad thematic patch, not a year-by-year campaign map or tax register.

In 1600 the Ming polygon owns nearly every tested mainland point. At 1715 the target vanishes and a larger Qing multipolygon owns its footprint. Neither seam proves one clean handover: the Ming capital fell in 1644, Southern Ming courts survived to 1662, the feudatory revolt ended in 1681 and Zheng Taiwan lasted to 1683.

sections.title: Unpack a label that bundles different regimes

items.text: Southern Ming means several rival courts that claimed continuation after Beijing fell, not one smoothly relocated government. The Yongli court became the last major inland claimant. Its emperor supplied dynastic legitimacy, while commanders with their own troops, treasuries and ambitions decided whether that legitimacy could travel farther than a ceremonial seal.

The Three Feudatories were former Ming commanders rewarded by the Qing with extraordinary southern autonomy. Wu Sangui’s Yunnan base, Shang family power in Guangdong and Geng family power in Fujian belonged to the conquest order they later attacked. Calling them simply Ming loyalists would reverse the reason their armies existed.

The Zheng maritime organization on the Fujian coast and Taiwan honored the Yongli era name and fought the Qing, but the target polygon excludes Xiamen and Tainan. Zheng history matters as a simultaneous loyalist path, not as permission to stretch this inland card across every anti-Qing sailor or Taiwanese community.

“Warlord” usefully signals commanders with personal armies, yet it can turn every official, soldier and local leader into a lawless strongman. Sun Kewang collected revenue and organized territory; Li Dingguo campaigned for the Yongli court; Wu Sangui first conquered for the Qing, then founded Zhou. Their careers demand verbs more exact than “warlorded.”

In late 1646 even Guangdong hosted competing Yongli and Shaowu courts, one at Zhaoqing and one at Guangzhou. Their contest ended quickly under Qing attack. That miniature civil war explains the larger problem: shared Ming ancestry did not automatically produce cooperation, and loyalist titles could multiply while usable soldiers and grain disappeared.

sections.title: Follow the Yongli court and its commanders

items.text: Sun Kewang and Li Dingguo had served the rebel Zhang Xianzhong before aligning with Yongli. Their experienced forces gave the court protection it could not create alone. The alliance also meant that men once branded rebels now carried Ming banners, a sharp reminder that survival politics could reorder loyalty faster than a court historian liked.

Sun moved the emperor to Anlong in 1652 and controlled the court there. Surviving source traditions are unusually rich for this phase, but they disagree in emphasis because later writers judged ambition, loyalty and betrayal. Calling Yongli either a free monarch or a decorative prisoner misses a relationship that changed under pressure.

Li Dingguo’s 1652 campaigns recovered Guilin and killed or defeated senior Qing commanders, briefly reversing the conquest across parts of Guangxi and Hunan. These were major military achievements, but victory did not repair divided command, exhausted supplies or fragile alliances. A spectacular battle could win a city and still lose the longer war.

Letters were political infrastructure. Courtiers sought allies, commanders sent orders and families searched for news, yet messengers crossed checkpoints and active fronts. A sealed letter might arrive late, be copied, intercepted or never arrive. Historians therefore read correspondence as evidence of both communication and the obstacles that warped it.

Jesuits at the fugitive court baptized several imperial relatives, including the empress dowager remembered as Helena, and European accounts turned their story into religious drama. Modern research corrects confused family relationships and exaggerated claims. It is a wonderful global connection, but it never made the whole Yongli court, army or southwest population Catholic.

sections.title: Watch Qing clients become Qing rebels

items.text: Wu Sangui helped the Qing enter Beijing in 1644 and later led conquest forces into the southwest. He seized Yongli from Burma and oversaw his execution. The same man then governed Yunnan with huge autonomy, showing why “Ming versus Qing” cannot explain every career: service, survival and personal power crossed that line repeatedly.

The feudatories maintained large armies and drew heavily on imperial revenue. Beijing valued their conquest experience but feared the cost and their independence. When the Kangxi government moved to abolish the domains in 1673, Wu revolted. A budget problem, succession problem and sovereignty problem suddenly became an eight-year civil war.

Wu’s revolt initially attracted officials and Green Standard commanders across several provinces. He declared a Zhou dynasty in 1678, an explicit new claim rather than a restored Ming reign. The choice made his earlier loyalist language even more complicated: opposition to Qing rule did not automatically mean putting a Zhu prince back on the throne.

Shang and Geng leaders joined, hesitated or surrendered at different moments. Qing commanders also varied in ability and loyalty. Treating both camps as solid colored chess teams hides desertion, negotiation and local calculation. For a town facing requisition, which banner approached could matter less than whether soldiers took grain, animals or labor.

After Wu died in 1678, the rebellion contracted toward Yunnan and ended in 1681. The Qing executed major feudatory leaders and dismantled their special powers. Victory strengthened imperial control, but it did not erase local chieftains, ethnic diversity, migration or memories of the Ming. Political consolidation and social uniformity are very different claims.

sections.title: Move armies, taxes, messages and supplies

items.text: Armies needed rice, fodder, powder, metal, pack animals, boats, porters and roads before they needed heroic speeches. Southern heat, mountain travel and disease complicated Qing campaigning, while local forces knew routes and supply points. Logistics explains why strong armies stalled and why civilians experienced war through requisitions long before a battle arrived.

Banner forces alone could not finish the feudatory war. The Qing increasingly depended on Green Standard troops led by Chinese officers, especially in the last southwest operations. This mixed conquest army undercuts a simple ethnic duel between Manchu attackers and Han defenders; people of several backgrounds fought on both sides.

Tax and grain systems could survive a change of ruler because every contender needed revenue. Yet the same household might face regular taxes, emergency levies, transport labor and soldiers demanding provisions. A neatly written quota does not tell us what collectors actually took, what elites avoided or what farmers hid.

The Lingqu Canal linked the Xiang and Li river systems between the Yangzi and Pearl watersheds using weirs, locks and controlled gradients. It long predated these wars, but its continuing transport and irrigation role shows how inherited infrastructure mattered. Commanders inherited clever waterways; they did not invent them between battles.

When postal routes collapsed in 1644, refugees, rumors, disease and agents crowded southbound roads. That crisis still shaped the world inherited in 1650. Movement was not only military: displaced families searched for safer towns, fields and patrons, while laborers and traders tried to keep local economies alive amid repeated regime demands.

sections.title: See a diverse southwest behind imperial claims

items.text: Yunnan, Guizhou, Guangxi and Guangdong were never one cultural block. Han settlers lived among many Yi, Miao, Yao, Zhuang, Dai and other communities whose own names and boundaries do not fit one imperial polygon. The card uses broad group names cautiously because court records often flattened peoples they sought to tax or command.

Many hereditary native officials, or tusi, governed through local authority while exchanging tribute and recognition with empires. Ming attempts to make tusi sons learn Confucian state norms did not automatically remake whole communities. Loyalty could be negotiated and layered, so an imperial seal did not mean a magistrate ran every upland household.

Lady Qu’s earlier Wuding inscriptions used both Nasu and Chinese to tell different stories of authority. Her example predates the card window, yet it proves that southwest elites strategically mastered more than one political language. Indigenous leaders were not passive translators waiting for an empire to explain who they were.

The shift from indirect tusi rule toward directly appointed officials varied by district and unfolded over centuries. Chinese descriptions of Guizhou often made conquest sound natural and complete. Reading those texts critically reveals how official vocabulary could turn contested incorporation into a tidy success story, much like a smooth atlas edge does.

Conquest restored or intensified unequal labor relations as well as political order. Bond servants, tenants, hired workers, porters and military households had different freedoms and risks. Elite accommodation often mattered more to regimes than emancipation below. The map’s giant color patch hides people whose legal status could decide whether moving was a choice.

sections.title: Find work, trade and knowledge amid war

items.text: Most people farmed, herded, carried goods or made things rather than attending court. Rural households combined subsistence with market work; women’s spinning and weaving could be central income, while men and women shared some seasonal farm tasks. Regional evidence varies, so no single “peasant day” fits coastal Guangdong and upland Yunnan.

In southern China rice commonly anchored meals, but fields and markets also supplied vegetables, fish, meat, fruit and prepared foods according to wealth and place. A museum set models an elaborate feast, not Tuesday lunch for every family. Funeral miniatures are evidence of food ideals, and perhaps proof that even ghosts received fancier menus.

Late Ming climate shocks and warfare drove grain prices to terrifying levels in some famines. Weather was never the only cause: armies, transport breakdown and hoarding changed access too. A harvest total can look adequate while a displaced household goes hungry because it lacks land, cash or protection on the road.

Jingdezhen porcelain workshops survived political fracture by changing patrons, designs and markets through 1620 to 1683. Their story belongs mostly outside this polygon, but it reveals a wider achievement of the transition: skilled production did not simply stop when dynasties changed. Kilns, traders and painters adapted while armies redrew allegiance.

Commercial print had expanded audiences for medicine, drama, fiction, genealogies and practical knowledge before the conquest. War destroyed some libraries and scattered readers, yet blocks, manuscripts and skills continued circulating. This was not a “warlord invention.” It was a resilient information system that competing regimes and communities inherited, used and censored.

sections.title: Meet families, children, schools and play

items.text: Households joined production, care, ancestor rites, marriage and property. Seventeenth-century commoner families increasingly organized lineages, but war and migration pulled members apart. Family did not always mean everyone slept under one roof; letters, remittances, shared ritual and property could hold together people living in different counties.

Migration often produced split families in which men traveled for soldiering, trade or work while women managed homes, farming and ritual obligations. Women could gain practical authority while remaining constrained by patriarchal law and chastity ideals. Calling that either full freedom or total seclusion would miss the difficult bargain.

Confucian education emphasized moral formation, classical texts and examinations. Schools, tutors and local academies served only part of the population, with girls less likely than boys to receive formal schooling. Children also learned farming, weaving, trading, ritual and craft skills at home, none of which appears on an exam roster.

Ming community-school orders promised local literacy and ethics instruction, but implementation depended on officials, gentry patrons and local resources. A village school’s existence did not make every child a student. War could remove teachers, books and fees just as surely as it removed soldiers, although families rebuilt learning networks afterward.

A famous palace painting shows twenty-two boys playing games, riding hobbyhorses and zooming down a masonry slide. It is much earlier and far more elite than an ordinary 1650 childhood, so it cannot supply a universal playground. Still, the hobbyhorse had one military advantage: it never demanded fodder.

sections.title: Eat, dress, live and socialize without one stereotype

items.text: Meals changed with ecology and income. Rice dominated many southern diets, but millet, tubers, vegetables, preserved foods, fish and occasional meat mattered locally. Feasts marked festivals, marriages, funerals and business. Hunger also shadowed wartime households, so a banquet image and a famine price belong in the same social history.

Clothing showed work, wealth, gender and political allegiance. Cotton and hemp served daily needs; silk and embroidered badges marked status. Late Ming portraits show women using rank imagery creatively, while Qing male hair rules made the queue a sign of submission. Getting dressed could become a political statement before breakfast.

Surviving Guizhou Tunpu settlements preserve stone, timber and earth courtyard traditions linked to Ming military migrants, plus irrigation and defensive planning. Buildings changed through repairs and later centuries, so they offer architectural continuity rather than a frozen 1650 house tour. Upland, town and coastal homes followed different materials and risks.

Markets and temple festivals offered exchange, worship, performance, gossip and marriage connections. Soldiers and refugees could enlarge a town one season and empty it the next. Court histories rarely count ordinary jokes, friendships or games, so social life must be reconstructed from objects, contracts, local texts and cautious comparison.

Ming loyalist artists turned landscape and calligraphy into intensely personal records of grief, refusal and identity. Their innovation was neither an escape from politics nor a government art program. Paintings preserve how some educated survivors made meaning after catastrophe, while reminding us that farmers, artisans and non-literate families left different archives.

sections.title: Test medicine, water, toilets, writing and the ending

items.text: A 1638 illustrated materia medica listed 452 substances with appearance, season, origin, applications and recipes. Practitioners also used pharmacies, household remedies and religious care. Printed classification was a serious knowledge achievement, but owning a book, finding a trained healer and affording ingredients were three very different things during war.

A Ming woodblock chart maps named acupuncture and moxibustion points across the head. Other epidemic responses included prescriptions, drug distribution, isolation, burial and ritual. These practices coexisted rather than forming one standardized hospital system. Children facing smallpox or fever could encounter skilled care, family treatment, prayer, nothing at all or several at once.

Yunnan communities had long built ponds, dams, ditches, sluices, bridges and granaries to manage crops and shortage. Those earlier works could survive rulers and support later households. No source proves every settlement had safe drinking water, however; irrigation, washing, firefighting and drinking drew on overlapping systems with unequal access and contamination risks.

No consulted source securely describes a typical 1650 southwest household toilet. Elsewhere in late imperial China, chamber pots, pits and night-soil collection linked towns to fertilizer markets. That comparison suggests possibilities, not a local blueprint. Human waste could be valuable “golden” fertilizer and still spread parasites: recycling was clever, while germ theory had not RSVP’d.

A Yongli copper cash coin reads “永曆通寶,” Yǒnglì tōngbǎo, “Circulating treasure of the Yongli reign.” Read top, bottom, right, left around the square hole, it is a four-character title, not a spoken sentence. The displayed Unicode is a normalized transcription, not a facsimile of one worn die. The 1715 atlas endpoint is not this regime’s fall: Yongli died in 1662 and the feudatory revolt ended in 1681.

ending.text: The target disappears at the 1715 atlas seam, but no historical “Post-Ming Warlords” state fell that year. The Yongli Southern Ming court ended politically with the emperor’s execution in 1662; the inland Three Feudatories rebellion ended in 1681; and the separate Zheng regime surrendered in 1683. By 1715 the audited footprint had long been governed within the Qing empire through provincial officials, garrisons and negotiated local authority. Families, communities, languages, religious life, farming, trade and memories of Ming loyalty continued. The card therefore records transformation at the map endpoint, sets fell to null and invents no direct successor link.
